title: Existentialism’s 21st‑Century Continuations - Cultural & Artistic Discourse
content_html:
Existentialism’s 21st‑Century Continuations - Cultural & Artistic Discourse

  • Language / Expression: Art as existential disclosure and narrative memory; prosthetic/postmemory across media.
  • Sleep / Replay / Dream: Symbolic recomposition in film, performance, and ritual; arts‑based approaches to impaired recall.
  • Meaning / Void / Infinite: Artistic creation as revolt/affirmation; cultural memory infrastructures in a platformed world.
  • Substrate: Media technologies as external memory carriers (photography, cinema, platforms).

Existentialist aesthetics

art reveals a world to others

Existentialist aesthetics treats art not as a self‑enclosed pursuit of form but as world‑disclosure: artworks reveal our situation to others and invite responsibility and action. This is a contemporary touchstone for reading artistic practice as memory‑work: artworks do not just depict memories but constitute how we remember together.

Cinema as an existential memory‑machine

Current scholarship revisits cinema as a laboratory for existential themes—authenticity, self‑deception, freedom—across classic and contemporary films. Special issues explicitly call for analyses of how film gives form to existential questions today. This frames cinema as a prosthetic and connective memory device that writes our shared pasts and possible selves.

Connective memory & platform culture

In the digital age, memory is increasingly connective: curated, circulated, and resurfaced by platforms. Reviews of digital memory studies show that feeds, rankings, and recommendation systems co‑author what cultures recall or forget, shifting from “collective memory” toward “connective/multitude memory.” This changes narrative identity and public remembrance.

Prosthetic memory & postmemory

taking on others’ pasts

Prosthetic memory (Landsberg) names memories acquired via mass media (film, museums) that become subjectively felt and ethically binding; postmemory (Hirsch) names inter‑/trans‑generational memory where descendants come to live with inherited trauma as if remembered. Both concepts have been reworked in the 2015–2025 period and remain central for understanding art as existential memory practice.

Aesthetic experience & transformation

Recent phenomenological studies show that being “moved by art” can be existentially transformative, entailing durable shifts in values and self‑narratives—effects mediated through memory encoding and later retrieval. Contemporary aesthetics also reframes the aesthetic experience in ways compatible with this transformative, memory‑laden account.

Arts‑based memory when recall fails

Arts‑based investigations in clinical/participatory settings demonstrate how scenic experience and embodied traces can be expressed visually despite impaired recall, suggesting artistic creation as an alternative memory pathway — highly relevant to memory replay and reconstruction.

Synthesis

  • Practice: Treat artworks as translation membranes that select, change, and reconstruct shared memory—especially in museums and online cultures.
  • Design: Use film/photography exhibits and digital archives to engineer retrieval cues for prosthetic/postmemorial engagement.
  • Ethics: Address authorship and responsibility in platformed remembrance; ensure contexts for existential meaning rather than mere virality.
